# Abstract {-}

Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has emerged as a powerful approach for characterizing cell-type-specific transcriptomes at high resolution across tissues and species. However, the bioinformatics analyses required to extract biological information from scRNA-seq datasets can be challenging for researchers without formal training in bioinformatics. Here, we provide a step-by-step workflow for inferring gene regulatory networks and pseudotime-based developmental trajectories from scRNA-seq data. To facilitate the implementation and reproducibility of these analyses, we provide a Docker image and a GitHub repository (github.com/laboratoriorgit-lang/SingleCell) containing all scripts, helper functions, reference files, container configuration, and environment YAML files. The workflow was applied to publicly available scRNA-seq data from *Arabidopsis thaliana* seedlings and enables the identification of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) across cell types, gene regulatory networks, and developmental trajectories associated with epidermal differentiation. Although this guide focuses on scRNA-seq analysis in *A. thaliana*, the workflow can be adapted to other organisms using appropriate reference genomes, genome annotations, and experimental designs.

\bigskip

**Key words:** scRNA-seq, gene regulatory networks, Differential gene expression, pseudotime-based trajectories.

\newpage

# Introduction

Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is a method that allows researchers to analyze the transcriptome of individual cells, thereby resolving cellular heterogeneity across tissues, developmental stages, and species (1-6). With single-cell resolution, it is possible to identify different cell identities and multiple states of the same cell type. This depth of molecular understanding provides a more precise understanding of their roles in growth and development of the plant (7). Briefly, single-cell RNA sequencing involves cells (such as protoplasts in plants) or individual nuclei isolation using droplet-based microfluidics and high-throughput technologies. Each droplet carries a DNA "barcode" that uniquely labels the cDNAs derived from a single cell. After the reverse transcription, the cDNAs from many cells are mixed for library preparation and RNA sequencing (8). The resulting sequencing data are processed computationally to generate a matrix of transcript counts, in which genes are quantified across individual cells. This matrix provides the basis for downstream analyses, including quality control, normalization, dimensionality reduction, clustering, cell-type identification and detection of differentially expressed genes (9). In addition, scRNA-seq data can also be used to investigate developmental relationships among cells through cell trajectories and inferring gene regulatory networks by integrating gene expression patterns with regulatory information (9).

Despite the potential of scRNA-seq, the computational analysis of these datasets requires integration of multiple bioinformatic tools and analytical steps. This complexity can represent a significant barrier for researchers with limited bioinformatics experience **(Fig. 1)**. In this chapter, we provide a step-by-step workflow for the analysis of scRNA-seq datasets, focusing on identification and characterization of cell populations, differential gene expression analysis, inference of gene regulatory networks, and reconstruction of pseudotime-based developmental trajectories. To make the setup easier, we provide all the software resources required to implement the workflow in a GitHub repository including a Docker image, scripts, helper functions, reference files, container configuration, and environment YAML files (github.com/laboratoriorgit-lang/SingleCell).

# Materials

1. A personal computer or server meeting the minimum computational requirements listed in **Table 1** is required to run the complete analysis pipeline described below. Small pilot datasets can be run on a laptop or desktop if memory is sufficient, starting from Step 2 onward. For full experiments, Cell Ranger processing from FASTQ, or large merged Seurat objects, a server or external cluster is strongly recommended.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{llrr}
\toprule
Stage & Component & Minimum & Recommended \\
\midrule
\textbf{Cell Ranger} (FASTQ $\rightarrow$ matrices) & CPU cores & 8 & 16+ \\
 & RAM & 64 GB & 128 GB \\
 & Disk space & 500 GB & 1 TB (FASTQ + BAM) \\
\textbf{R/Seurat} (Section 2+) & CPU cores & 4 & 8+ \\
 & RAM & 8 GB & 32 GB \\
 & Disk space & 80 GB & 100 GB \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\small
**Table 1. Minimum computational requirements for running the complete analysis pipeline on a personal computer or server.**
\normalsize

2. The software required for downstream analyses is provided in a Docker container image (psblab/scrnaseq). A container image is a standardized package containing the files, executables, libraries, and configuration settings required to run software in a consistent and reproducible environment. This container image can be run using either Docker or Singularity (now known as Apptainer), depending on the operating system and computing environment. Both platforms support Docker container images, but differ in their architecture and security models. Docker typically relies on a daemon that runs with root privileges and uses layered filesystems. In contrast, Singularity/Apptainer operates without a privileged daemon and allows containers to run with the permissions of the host user. It can also convert Docker images into a single, portable, and immutable Singularity Image Format (.sif) file. These characteristics make Singularity/Apptainer particularly suitable for shared high-performance computing (HPC) environments, where users generally do not have root privileges.

3. ScRNA-seq data may be found on public databases or obtained in-house. Here we use RNA-seq information from *Arabidopsis thaliana* described in Han et al., 2023 (10), published in *Nature Plants* and deposited at the China National Center for Bioinformation (<https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/>) Genome Sequence Archive under BioProject PRJCA016521, run accession CRA010863 (<https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/bioproject/browse/PRJCA016521>).

# Methods

The following sections describe a step-by-step workflow for inferring gene regulatory networks (GRNs) and reconstructing pseudotime-based developmental trajectories from single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data **(Figure 1)**. The pipeline guides users from raw Cell Ranger processing through QC, integration, clustering, cell-type annotation, pseudobulk differential expression, GO enrichment, gene co-expression, regulatory network inference, and pseudotime trajectory reconstruction.

This workflow is designed for researchers without formal training in bioinformatics and provides a starting point for incorporating scRNA-seq data analysis into a research project.

\newpage

## Step 1 - Initial set up and raw data acquisition {-}

### Step 1.1. Creating a persistent terminal session with tmux {-}

Before running the pipeline, we recommend starting a persistent terminal session using tmux. tmux is a tool that allows you to keep computational tasks running in the background. Several steps in the workflow may take a long time to complete and do not require user interaction. If your SSH connection is interrupted or you close the terminal, tmux allows these processes to continue running in the background, provided the machine remains available and running. Install tmux using the instructions for your operating system (<https://github.com/tmux/tmux/wiki/Installing>).

Once tmux is installed, create a new named session by running the following command. The “tmux” command launches the Terminal Multiplexer, “new” creates a new session, and “-s” allows you to assign a custom name to that session. In this example, “scrnaseq” is the name given to the session, making it easier to identify and manage throughout the analysis workflow.

```bash
tmux new -s scrnaseq
```

If you need to reconnect to a previously created session, run the following command. The “attach” option allows you to reconnect to an existing session, while “-t” specifies the target session you want to access. In this example, “scrnaseq” is the name of the session you want to resume.

```bash
tmux attach -t scrnaseq
```

If you need to know the list of running sessions, you can use the following command line. It allows you to quickly verify which work environments are alive, check if your background pipelines are still running, and see their exact names.

```bash
tmux ls
```

### Step 1.2. Clone the repository {-}

To facilitate further processing, we will first choose or create a working directory. Then, we will clone the pipeline repository into the working directory.

```bash
mkdir -p ~/my-analysis
cd ~/my-analysis
git clone https://github.com/laboratoriorgit-lang/SingleCell.git
cd SingleCell
```

### Step 1.3. Starting the software environment {-}

In this workflow, we recommend using Singularity/Apptainer because it is particularly well suited for shared computing environments, such as university servers and high-performance computing (HPC) clusters. First, users must install Singularity/Apptainer, a container platform for running portable software environments. Singularity/Apptainer version 1.5.4 can be installed using different methods, depending on the operating system. Follow the installation instructions for your operating system provided in the official Apptainer documentation <https://apptainer.org/docs/admin/main/installation.html#install-from-source>.

**i\) Build the container image.** This step converts the public Docker Hub image into a local Singularity Image Format (.sif) file. It only needs to be performed once per machine, unless the image needs to be updated.

```bash
singularity build scrnaseq.sif docker://psblab/scrnaseq:latest
```

**ii\) Run the container.** Execute the following command to start an interactive Bash shell inside the container. Bash is a command-line interpreter that allows users to execute commands and interact with the operating system through a terminal. By starting a Bash shell inside the container, users can directly access the software and tools installed in the container environment. The command also binds the current working directory on the host computer to /workspace inside the container and sets /workspace as the working directory. This allows users to access their project files from within the container without having to copy them.

```bash
singularity exec --bind $(pwd):/workspace --pwd /workspace scrnaseq.sif /bin/bash
```

**Optional.** If you encounter problems running the Singularity/Apptainer container, you can use Docker as an alternative. However, Docker typically requires root privileges or membership in the docker group, which may not be available on shared computing systems. For this reason, Docker is not the default option in this workflow.

### Step 1.4. Raw data download and Cell Ranger processing {-}

**i\) Download Cell Ranger**

Before installing Singularity/Docker, users must download and install Cell Ranger, a software suite developed by 10x Genomics for processing single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data. Cell Ranger processes raw FASTQ reads and generates gene expression count matrices for further analysis. To obtain the software, visit <https://www.10xgenomics.com/software>. Please note this pipeline was run with Cell Ranger version 9.0.1. Please follow the company’s download and installation instructions for this version. Once you get to the URL to download the software, copy the download command provided on the 10x Genomics website to download from the terminal as indicated below:

```bash
curl -o cellranger-9.0.1.tar.gz "PASTE_DOWNLOAD_URL_HERE"
```

The following commands unpack the file and install Cell Ranger 9.0.1. The “export PATH” command adds the Cell Ranger installation directory to the system's search path. This allows you to run cellranger from any working directory without specifying its full installation path. To verify that Cell Ranger is correctly configured, run `cellranger --version`. The command should display the installed version number. If you see a command not found message, it means that the PATH variable has not been set correctly.

```bash
tar -xzvf cellranger-9.0.1.tar.gz
export PATH=$PWD/cellranger-9.0.1/bin:$PATH
cellranger --version
```

**ii\) Downloading public scRNA-seq data**

The dataset used in this chapter is described in Han et al. (2023), and is publicly available through the China National Center for Bioinformation (<https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/>) Genome Sequence Archive under BioProject PRJCA016521 and GSA accession CRA010863.

The original dataset includes multiple experimental conditions and samples. To simplify the workflow and facilitate the demonstration of the analysis pipeline, we selected scRNA-seq data from two genotypes of *Arabidopsis thaliana*: wild-type (WT) and the *pifq* mutant **(Table 2)**.

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
Sample & Run accession & Files \\
\midrule
ScWT & CRR775298 & \begin{tabular}[t]{@{}l@{}}\texttt{CRR775298\_f1.fastq.gz,}\\ \texttt{CRR775298\_r2.fastq.gz}\end{tabular} \\[6pt]
Scpifq & CRR775297 & \begin{tabular}[t]{@{}l@{}}\texttt{CRR775297\_f1.fastq.gz,}\\ \texttt{CRR775297\_r2.fastq.gz}\end{tabular} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
```

\small
**Table 2. scRNA-seq datasets selected for the analysis workflow.** To simplify the workflow and facilitate the demonstration of the analysis pipeline, we selected samples from two *Arabidopsis thaliana* genotypes.
\normalsize

Download the corresponding raw sequencing data from the public repository. Depending on the file sizes and network connection, this step may take considerable time. After downloading the raw sequencing data, rename the FASTQ files or create symbolic links using the naming convention expected by Cell Ranger: `<sample>_S1_L001_R1_001.fastq.gz` for Read 1 and `<sample>_S1_L001_R2_001.fastq.gz` for Read 2 (see Note 1). This convention allows Cell Ranger to identify the sample name and distinguish the two read files during processing.

```bash
mkdir -p /workspace/fastq/CRA010863

wget -c -P /workspace/fastq/CRA010863 \
  ftp://download.big.ac.cn/gsa2/CRA010863/CRR775298/CRR775298_f1.fastq.gz
wget -c -P /workspace/fastq/CRA010863 \
  ftp://download.big.ac.cn/gsa2/CRA010863/CRR775298/CRR775298_r2.fastq.gz
wget -c -P /workspace/fastq/CRA010863 \
  ftp://download.big.ac.cn/gsa2/CRA010863/CRR775297/CRR775297_f1.fastq.gz
wget -c -P /workspace/fastq/CRA010863 \
  ftp://download.big.ac.cn/gsa2/CRA010863/CRR775297/CRR775297_r2.fastq.gz

cd /workspace/fastq/CRA010863
ln -s CRR775298_f1.fastq.gz ScWT_S1_L001_R1_001.fastq.gz
ln -s CRR775298_r2.fastq.gz ScWT_S1_L001_R2_001.fastq.gz
ln -s CRR775297_f1.fastq.gz Scpifq_S1_L001_R1_001.fastq.gz
ln -s CRR775297_r2.fastq.gz Scpifq_S1_L001_R2_001.fastq.gz
```

**iii) Building the Cell Ranger reference**

To align scRNA-seq reads and quantify gene expression, a reference transcriptome must first be generated for Cell Ranger. In this workflow, the TAIR10.1 reference genome and Araport11 gene annotation are included in compressed form in the container setup; therefore, users do not need to download these files separately.

Decompress the reference genome and annotation files, then build the Cell Ranger reference package using the `cellranger mkref` command (see Note 2). This step generates the reference files required for subsequent read alignment and gene expression quantification.

```bash
gunzip -k data/Arabidopsis_thaliana_TAIR10.1_Araport11_genome.fasta.gz
gunzip -k data/Arabidopsis_thaliana_TAIR10.1_Araport11_annotation.gtf.gz

cellranger mkref \
  --genome=Ara \
  --fasta=data/Arabidopsis_thaliana_TAIR10.1_Araport11_genome.fasta \
  --genes=data/Arabidopsis_thaliana_TAIR10.1_Araport11_annotation.gtf
```

**iv) Running Cell Ranger count**

Next, run `cellranger count` for each sample to align the sequencing reads to the reference genome and generate gene expression count matrices (see Note 3). The `--localcores` parameter controls the number of CPU cores allocated to Cell Ranger. Adjust this value according to the number of CPU cores available on the machine running the analysis. Increasing the number of cores may reduce processing time, provided that sufficient computational resources are available. Avoid allocating more cores than the system can support, particularly when running multiple samples in parallel.

```bash
cellranger count --localcores=10 --id=ScWT --fastqs=/workspace/fastq/CRA010863 \
  --sample=ScWT --transcriptome=Ara --create-bam false

cellranger count --localcores=10 --id=Scpifq --fastqs=/workspace/fastq/CRA010863 \
  --sample=Scpifq --transcriptome=Ara --create-bam false
```

Before moving on, inspect the Cell Ranger output for both samples. Problems with sequencing quality or cell calling are easier to identify at this stage than after clustering. Open `ScWT/outs/web_summary.html` and `Scpifq/outs/web_summary.html` in a web browser. The same key metrics are available in `outs/metrics_summary.csv`.

## Step 2. Single-cell analysis in R {-}

### Step 2.1. Initialization {-}

In the following steps, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data will be analyzed using R within the Singularity/Docker container.

```r
R
```

**Note:** The processed Cell Ranger outputs for both samples are included in the repository. Therefore, this workflow can start directly from the processed count matrices, without repeating Step 1 (FASTQ download and Cell Ranger processing).

In this step, we generated `init_pipeline()` and `source()` functions that contain the pipeline helper scripts, a fixed random seed to support reproducibility, Seurat compatibility options, the R session to the project working directory, and the output directories required for subsequent analyses. Seurat is an R package designed for QC, analysis, and exploration of single-cell RNA-seq data (11).

Once this initialization step is complete, the R session is configured and ready to execute the subsequent analysis steps.

```r
source("/workspace/workflow/init.R")
init_pipeline(data_dir = "/workspace/.", seed = 1807)
```

### Step 2.2. Quality control and cell filtering {-}

In this step, we load the gene-expression count matrices generated by Cell Ranger for each sample and assess their quality before downstream analysis. The pipeline generates quality-control (QC) plots before filtering **(Figure 2)**, removes low-quality cells and potential doublets, and then generates a second set of plots to evaluate the results of filtering **(Figure 3)**.

Several parameters can be adjusted to match the characteristics of your experiment, including sample IDs, sample colors, mitochondrial gene patterns, minimum number of detected genes (`min_features`), maximum mitochondrial transcript percentage (`max_mt`), and whether to run DoubletFinder (`run_doubletfinder`).

**i) Define your samples.** Edit the sample list so that it contains one entry for each sample included in your experiment. Each entry requires three pieces of information:

- `file`: The path to the `filtered_feature_bc_matrix` folder generated by Cell Ranger, relative to `DATA_DIR`. This folder contains the gene expression count matrix used for downstream analysis.
- `label`: A short, unique sample name used to identify the sample in plots and analysis objects. Choose labels that are easy to recognize and use them consistently throughout the workflow.
- `condition`: The experimental group or treatment associated with the sample, such as wild-type (WT) or *pifq*. This information will help you compare samples or experimental conditions during downstream analyses.

**ii) Define sample colors.** Assign one color to each sample label. Using consistent colors makes it easier to distinguish samples in QC plots and subsequent visualizations, particularly when comparing biological replicates or experimental conditions.

**iii) Identify mt patterns.** The pipeline uses gene name patterns to identify mitochondrial genes. In *Arabidopsis thaliana*, mitochondrial genes typically have identifiers beginning with ATMG. This pattern is used as the default settings in this workflow. Correctly identifying these genes is important because the proportion of organellar transcripts can provide useful information about cell quality and sample characteristics.

**iv) min_features.** This parameter defines the minimum number of genes that a cell must express to be retained for downstream analysis. Cells with very few detected genes may represent empty droplets or low-quality cells with insufficient RNA content. Increasing this threshold removes more cells, whereas decreasing it retains cells with lower gene-detection complexity. The threshold should be selected based on the distribution of detected genes in your dataset.

**v) max_mt.** This parameter defines the maximum percentage of mitochondrial transcripts allowed in each cell. Cells exceeding this threshold are removed because a high proportion of mitochondrial transcripts can indicate cellular damage or poor RNA quality. However, mitochondrial transcript levels can vary across tissues and cell types, so the threshold should be evaluated using the QC plots rather than applied as a universal cutoff.

**vi) run_doubletfinder:** a doublet occurs when two cells are captured and processed together as a single cell barcode. As a result, the expression profile may contain transcripts from two distinct cell types, potentially creating artificial cell populations or affecting downstream clustering and gene regulatory network inference. DoubletFinder identifies potential doublets computationally based on similarities between observed cells and simulated doublets. Its predictions should be interpreted as estimates rather than definitive classifications.

```r
samples <- list(
  list(file = "ScWT/outs/filtered_feature_bc_matrix",
       label = "WT", condition = "WT"),
  list(file = "Scpifq/outs/filtered_feature_bc_matrix",
       label = "pifq", condition = "pifq")
)

colors <- c("WT" = "#66c2a5", "pifq" = "#fc8d62")

seurat_list <- run_qc_filtering(
  samples, colors,
  mt_pattern        = "^ATMG",
  min_features      = 200,
  max_mt            = 5,
  run_doubletfinder = TRUE
)
```

### Step 2.3. UMAP and Harmony integration {-}

In this step, the filtered samples are combined into a single Seurat object, followed by data normalization, dimensionality reduction, and batch correction. The workflow first generates a UMAP visualization before batch correction **(Figure 4)** and then applies Harmony to reduce technical differences between samples, followed by a second UMAP visualization **(Figure 5)**.

The workflow first normalizes gene expression data to account for differences in sequencing depth between cells. It then identifies highly variable genes (HVG), which capture informative expression differences across cells, and scales the expression matrix to prepare it for downstream analyses. Next, the workflow performs principal component analysis (PCA), which summarizes the major patterns of variation in gene expression into a smaller number of dimensions called principal components (PCs). The principal components are then used to generate a uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP). UMAP is a dimensionality reduction method that represents cells in a two-dimensional map based on similarities in their gene-expression profiles. Each point represents a cell, and cells with more similar expression profiles tend to appear closer together. This visualization helps researchers identify groups of cells with similar molecular characteristics **(Figure 4)**.

```r
ath_sc <- run_umap_integration(
  seurat_list, colors,
  nfeatures = 2000,
  npcs      = 30,
  dims      = 1:30
)
```

\bigskip

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.55\linewidth]{assets/fig4_umap_preharmony.png}
\end{center}

\small
**Figure 4. UMAP visualization before Harmony integration, colored by sample identity.** The plot shows the distribution of cells from wild-type (WT) and *pifq* mutant samples before batch-effect correction, illustrating sample-specific clustering patterns and potential differences in cell distribution.
\normalsize

Samples processed or sequenced separately can show differences that are unrelated to the underlying biology. These technical differences, commonly referred to as batch effects, may arise from sample preparation, cell capture, library construction, or sequencing depth (12). If these effects are not addressed, cells may cluster according to their sample of origin rather than their cell type or biological characteristics, potentially complicating downstream analyses.

Harmony uses the sample identity information stored in the dataset to identify and correct sample-specific differences (batch effects) in the principal component (PC) space (13). This correction reduces technical variation between samples, improving the comparability of cells across samples while aiming to preserve biologically meaningful differences in gene expression. As a result, cells with similar transcriptional profiles can be grouped together regardless of their sample of origin.

After Harmony correction, the workflow recalculates the UMAP visualization using the corrected representation **(Figure 5)**. Compare this visualization with the pre-Harmony UMAP generated in this step. Improved mixing of cells from different samples within corresponding cell populations may indicate that sample-associated variation has been reduced. At the same time, biologically distinct cell populations should remain distinguishable.

Keep in mind that better sample mixing does not automatically mean that the correction was successful. Genuine biological differences between samples or experimental conditions should not be removed. Therefore, interpret the corrected UMAP alongside the original visualization and the experimental design.

The UMAP plots by sample before and after Harmony are saved to `results/01_qc/`, and the objects `ath_sc_preharmony.rds` and `ath_sc_postharmony.rds` to `results/objects/`. These outputs are used in the subsequent analysis steps.

\bigskip

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.55\linewidth]{assets/fig5_umap_postharmony.png}
\end{center}

\small
**Figure 5. UMAP visualization after Harmony integration, colored by sample identity.** The plot shows the distribution of cells from wild-type (WT) and *pifq* mutant samples following batch-effect correction with Harmony, allowing assessment of sample mixing and the effectiveness of batch-effect correction.
\normalsize

### Step 2.4. Clustering resolution and final clustering {-}

At this stage, the samples have been merged and batch-corrected. Before identifying cell populations, we need to make two important decisions: how many principal components (PCs) to include in the analysis and which clustering resolution to use. These parameters influence how cells are grouped according to similarities in their gene-expression profiles. To help guide these decisions, we have prepared the `run_clustering()` function, which generates three visualizations: an elbow plot **(Figure 6)**, a clustree plot **(Figure 7)**, and a UMAP showing the resulting cell clusters **(Figure 8)**.

In this workflow, we selected a resolution of 0.35. The clustree visualization indicates a relatively stable clustering structure at this resolution, with most clusters showing clear correspondence to clusters at the preceding resolution. However, the choice of resolution is not universal and should be guided by the dataset, clustering stability, and expected biological diversity.

```r
ath_sc <- run_clustering(
  ath_sc,
  resolutions_test   = c(0.15, 0.35, 0.45, 0.55, 1.0),
  cluster_resolution = 0.35,
  dims               = 1:30
)
```

Once these parameters have been defined, the workflow performs Leiden clustering and assigns each cell a numerical cluster identifier, stored in the Seurat metadata column `seurat_clusters` **(Figure 8)**. These cluster IDs provide the starting point for cell-type annotation in the next section. The resulting elbow plots and clustree are saved in `results/02_clustering/` and then clusters the cells at `cluster_resolution` (Section 6), saving the UMAP of the clusters.

**Figure 8. UMAP visualization of Seurat cell clusters.** Cells are colored according to their assigned cluster identities, with each cluster represented by a unique number. Clustering was performed using the selected resolution, allowing visualization of the transcriptionally distinct cell populations identified in the dataset.
\normalsize

### Step 2.5. Cell-type annotation and gene expression {-}

In this section, we assign biological identities to the clusters identified in the previous step. To interpret these clusters, we use marker genes reported in the scientific literature as references for identifying known cell populations. The marker gene reference table is provided in `data/biblio_marks.txt`. The marker gene table contains one row per marker gene and three required columns: i) `celltype`: the cell type associated with the marker, ii) `symbol`: the gene symbol, and `ID`: the gene identifier, using the *Arabidopsis thaliana* AGI locus code. These identifiers must match the gene names used in the Seurat object.

The `run_annotation()` function incorporates Seurat's `FindAllMarkers()` function to identify marker genes that are differentially expressed in each cluster compared with all other cells. To assign cell-type identities, the pipeline compares the significant marker genes identified for each cluster with a reference list of marker genes compiled from the scientific literature (`biblio_marks.txt`). When a match is found, the annotation function selects the reference marker with the lowest adjusted p-value and assigns its corresponding cell-type label to the cluster. If the same cell-type label is assigned to multiple clusters, a numerical suffix is added to distinguish them (e.g., Mesophyll.1 and Mesophyll.2). A dotplot is generated to assess whether the expected marker genes support the proposed annotations, while a UMAP plot displays the resulting cell-type labels across the dataset. In a dot plot, the color typically represents average gene expression, while the dot size indicates the proportion of cells expressing each gene. Together, these features help assess whether the selected markers are consistent with the assigned identities **(Figure 9)**.

**Interpretation:** Treat the assigned labels as putative cell identities rather than definitive classifications. Marker expression can vary between cell types, developmental stages, and experimental conditions. Whenever possible, use multiple marker genes and consider the biological context to validate each annotation.

In addition, we can visualize the expression of a selected gene across the annotated cell types. This allows you to explore where a gene is expressed, compare its expression levels between cell populations, and assess whether its expression pattern is consistent with its known or expected biological function. As an example, we used AT4G21750 (*ATML1*), a well-established marker gene for epidermal cells in *Arabidopsis*, to illustrate the identification and visualization of cell-type-specific gene expression. The pipeline generates two complementary visualizations: a Violin plot, which shows the distribution of *ATML1* expression across cell clusters, and a FeaturePlot, which displays its expression pattern across cells in the UMAP embedding. Together, these plots illustrate how marker gene expression can be used to support cell-type annotation **(Figure 10)**. Keep in mind that low or undetected expression does not necessarily indicate that a gene is biologically inactive, as transcript detection can be affected by sequencing depth and the inherent sparsity of scRNA-seq data. The resulting figures are saved in `results/03_annotation/` and `results/04_expression/`.

```r
ath_sc <- run_annotation(
  ath_sc,
  marker_file = "data/biblio_marks.txt",
  gene        = "AT4G21750"
)
```

### Step 2.6. Exporting the curated Seurat object {-}

This final step of the R workflow exports the curated Seurat object in two formats to support downstream analyses in both R and Python. The `.rds` file preserves the R object for future use in Seurat, whereas the `.h5ad` file provides an AnnData-compatible representation for analysis with Python-based tools.

```r
run_export_object(ath_sc, name = "ath_sc_annotated")
```

Both files are saved in `results/objects/`:

- `ath_sc_annotated.rds`: the curated Seurat object for subsequent analyses in R.
- `ath_sc_annotated.h5ad`: the corresponding AnnData object for downstream analyses in Python.

Before proceeding, verify that both files were generated successfully. Because conversion between Seurat and AnnData objects may not preserve every data structure or metadata field identically, check that the relevant expression data, cell annotations, dimensionality reductions, and other required metadata are available in the exported object before using it in subsequent analyses.

## Step 3. Pseudobulk differential expression and GO {-}

This chapter continues the workflow using the curated single-cell object generated at the end of step 2. Cells are aggregated into pseudobulk profiles for each cell type and biological replicate, enabling differential expression analysis with DESeq2 to compare the wild-type (WT) and *pifq* mutant genotypes. The results are summarized using volcano plots and differential expression tables, followed by Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis, a log~2~ fold-change heatmap, and co-expression network analysis. Together, these analyses identify cell-type-specific transcriptional differences between WT and *pifq* and provide complementary approaches for interpreting the biological processes and gene relationships associated with the mutant phenotype.

```r
ath_sc <- readRDS(file.path(dir_objects, "ath_sc_annotated.rds"))
```

### Step 3.1. Assigning pseudo-replicates {-}

The `run_pseudobulk_de()` function performs differential gene expression analysis using a pseudobulk approach. First, it assigns pseudo-replicates to cells within each cell type and condition. The number of pseudo-replicates is controlled by the `n_pseudoreps` parameter. In this workflow, we set `n_pseudoreps = 3`, meaning that cells belonging to each cell type and condition are divided into three groups, provided that a sufficient number of cells is available. Cell types that do not contain cells from both conditions required for a given comparison (e.g., cell types detected in only one condition) are excluded from that differential expression analysis.

For each cell type, aggregated gene counts are analyzed using methods developed for bulk RNA-seq data and implemented in DESeq2 (14). The comparisons are defined using the `comparisons` parameter, in which each entry specifies the two conditions to be compared and a corresponding tag. For each cell type and comparison, the pipeline generates a DESeq2 results table containing one row per gene. In this workflow, we applied a log~2~ fold-change threshold of 1 and an adjusted p-value threshold of 0.05 to identify differentially expressed genes. The results are visualized using volcano plots **(Figure 11)**, which highlight genes with significant expression changes, and log~2~ fold-change heatmaps **(Figure 12)**, which facilitate the comparison of expression patterns across cell types and conditions. The `heatmap_limits` parameter sets the limits of the color scale. In this workflow, the range is set from $-5$ to $5$, allowing negative and positive log~2~ fold changes to be displayed on a common scale.

To identify biological processes associated with the differentially expressed genes in each cell type, the pipeline also performs Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis **(Figure 13)**. The `go_space` parameter specifies the GO category to be analyzed. In this workflow, it is set to `BP` (Biological Process). The organism annotation database is specified using `go_orgdb`, while `go_keytype` defines the gene identifier format used to map genes to the database. For *Arabidopsis thaliana*, these parameters are set to `org.At.tair.db` and `TAIR`, respectively. The resulting differential expression tables and visualizations are saved in `results/06_de_results/`, while GO enrichment results are saved in `results/07_go/`.

```r
de <- run_pseudobulk_de(
  ath_sc,
  marker_file    = "data/biblio_marks.txt",
  comparisons    = list(
    list(conds = c("WT", "pifq"), tag = "WT_vs_pifq")
  ),
  annot_col      = "celltype",
  n_pseudoreps   = 3,
  padj_cut       = 0.05,
  lfc_cut        = 1,
  go_space       = "BP",
  go_orgdb       = org.At.tair.db,
  go_keytype     = "TAIR",
  heatmap_limits = c(-5, 5)
)
```

### Step 3.2. Gene co-expression and transcription factor networks {-}

To investigate gene regulatory networks under PIFQ regulation, the pipeline integrates single-cell transcriptomic data with information on transcription factor (TF)–target gene interactions. This analysis uses hdWGCNA to construct gene co-expression networks from scRNA-seq data and identify potential relationships between TFs and their target genes. By combining gene co-expression patterns with regulatory information, this approach helps identify candidate regulatory relationships and explore how PIFQ influences gene expression across different cell types.

hdWGCNA is an extension of weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) adapted for single-cell and single-nucleus RNA-seq datasets (15). It identifies groups of genes, known as co-expression modules, that exhibit similar expression patterns across cells. These modules can reveal coordinated gene expression programs associated with specific cell types or biological conditions.

For simplicity and reproducibility, all hdWGCNA commands required for this analysis, together with the transcription factor list, are implemented in the `run_tf_network()` function. The function includes several parameters that control network construction and visualization, including the number of metacells used to reduce data sparsity, the minimum module size, the `deepSplit` parameter for controlling module detection sensitivity, the TOM threshold, and the number of hub transcription factors labeled in the final network **(Figure 14)**.

```r
run_tf_network(
  ath_sc,
  contrast_tag    = "WT_vs_pifq",
  annot_col       = "celltype",
  tf_list         = "data/AtTFDB_loci.txt",
  n_metacells     = 50,
  min_module_size = 20,
  deep_split      = 2,
  soft_power      = NULL,
  tom_threshold   = 0.2,
  n_hub_label     = 15
)
```

The resulting network files are saved in `results/08_networks/`. In particular, the `TF_TARGET_interaccion.tsv` file contains the inferred network edges and can be imported into Cytoscape for network visualization and further analysis. For a detailed, step-by-step introduction to gene co-expression network construction and its application to *Arabidopsis thaliana* RNA-seq data, readers are referred to Contreras-López et al. (2018) (16). This resource provides additional methodological guidance on network construction, analysis, and biological interpretation.

## Step 4. Pseudotime trajectory analysis {-}

Single-cell transcriptomics provides a powerful approach to understanding the dynamics underlying biological processes, such as cell differentiation or transitions between cellular states. Expression-based trajectory inference methods explore variation among cellular states by using similarities in their gene-expression profiles to reconstruct the trajectories (17) while pseudotime assigns each cell a relative position along this inferred progression. Together, these approaches allow researchers to identify genes whose expression patterns change across cellular states.

Two key steps in trajectory inference are dimensionality reduction and root selection, both of which influence the inferred trajectory and its biological interpretation. While previous clustering process aims to identify distinct cell populations, trajectory inference focuses on their relationships and potential transitions between cellular states. Different methods use distinct approaches to reconstruct these trajectories. For example, Monocle 3 learns a trajectory graph from a UMAP representation (18), whereas diffusion-based approaches capture relationships between cellular states across multiple scales (19). Root selection determines the direction of pseudotime and should ideally be guided by biological knowledge, such as known progenitor populations or marker genes.

In this workflow, we use a diffusion-based approach to reconstruct cellular trajectories. Starting from the PCA performed in Step 2, we used Palantir (19) to generate a multiscale diffusion map that captures relationships between transcriptional states. We then use scFates (20) to fit a principal tree to this representation, reconstruct potential branching trajectories, and assign pseudotime based on a selected root. The workflow starts from the annotated AnnData object exported at the end of Step 2, `results/objects/ath_sc_annotated.h5ad`. To continue, exit the R session and start Python within the same software container. This allows you to use the Python environment and packages configured for the pipeline without leaving the container.

```r
q()          # leave R (do not save the workspace)
```

```bash
python3
```

### Step 4.1. Setting up the Python environment {-}

This step initializes the Python environment required for trajectory analysis. It defines the project paths established in the previous steps of the pipeline, loads the necessary Python packages and helper scripts, and creates the output directory for pseudotime analyses.

The first command loads the `init_pipeline()` function from `init.py`. The second command runs `init_pipeline()`, which performs these initialization tasks by loading the required Python packages and helper scripts and creating the pseudotime output directory.

```python
exec(open("/workspace/workflow/init.py").read(), globals())
init_pipeline(data_dir="/workspace/.")
```

### Step 4.2. Loading the annotated AnnData object {-}

This step loads the `.h5ad` object exported at the end of the R workflow. The `INPUT_H5AD` variable specifies the path to the input file, while `ANNOTATION_COL` selects the cell-type annotation column used to visualize the data and select cells for trajectory analysis.

Depending on which optional annotation steps were completed in step 2, the object may contain up to three annotation columns:

- `celltype`: the original annotation generated in Step 2.5 using literature-based marker genes. This column is always present.
- `celltype_grouped`: available if Supplementary Section S1 was run. Related subclusters are merged into broader cell-type groups.
- `celltype_curated`: available if Supplementary Section S2 was run. This column contains manually reviewed and curated cell-type labels.

Set `ANNOTATION_COL` according to the annotation workflow used in Step 2:

- Use `celltype` if neither Supplementary Section S1 nor S2 was performed.
- Use `celltype_grouped` if only Supplementary Section S1 was performed.
- Use `celltype_curated` if Supplementary Section S2 was performed.

The example in this workflow uses `celltype`. With the current marker table, the cotyledon epidermis is represented by a single label, `Epidermis Cotyledon`, which will be used in Step 4.3 and 4.4.

The loading function also standardizes the coordinate names in the object to ensure compatibility with Scanpy. It prints the available annotation columns so you can verify that `ANNOTATION_COL` matches a column in the loaded object. Finally, it generates an overview UMAP and lists the available cell types. Use this information to select the appropriate cell population for trajectory analysis in the next step.

```python
INPUT_H5AD = "/workspace/results/objects/ath_sc_annotated.h5ad"
ANNOTATION_COL = "celltype"
N_JOBS = 4

adata, N_JOBS = load_curated_object(
    input_h5ad=INPUT_H5AD,
    dir_pseudotime=dir_pseudotime,
    annotation_col=ANNOTATION_COL,
    n_jobs=N_JOBS,
)
```

### Step 4.3. Selecting cell types for trajectory inference {-}

This step specifies which cell types will be included in the trajectory analysis. The selected populations are defined in `TRAJECTORY_CLUSTERS`, and each entry must exactly match a cell-type label displayed in Step 4.2.

In this workflow, trajectory inference is performed on the epidermis cotyledon, identified by the label `Epidermis Cotyledon` in the current marker table. A preview UMAP is generated to visualize the selected cells before trajectory inference, allowing you to confirm that the intended population has been selected **(Figure 15)**.

```python
TRAJECTORY_CLUSTERS = ["Epidermis Cotyledon"]

adata_sub = preview_trajectory_selection(
    adata=adata,
    clusters=TRAJECTORY_CLUSTERS,
    annotation_col=ANNOTATION_COL,
    dir_pseudotime=dir_pseudotime,
)
```

If you used the optional annotation grouping or manual curation steps (Supplementary Sections S1 and S2) in Step 2, ensure that `ANNOTATION_COL` is set to the corresponding column in Step 4.2. The labels specified in `TRAJECTORY_CLUSTERS` must match the labels in that selected annotation column.

Restricting the analysis to a biologically relevant cell population can help characterize developmental or transcriptional trajectories without combining cell types that are not within the same lineage. However, the selected population should contain sufficient cells and transcriptional variation to support meaningful trajectory inference.

\end{center}

\small
**Figure 15. UMAP visualization of epidermis cotyledon cells selected for trajectory inference.** The UMAP displays the distribution of the selected cell population, providing a visual quality check to confirm that the intended cell type was correctly identified before trajectory inference.
\normalsize

### Step 4.4. Trajectory inference and root selection {-}

This step fits a pseudotime trajectory to the selected cells and determines its root, which defines the starting point for ordering cells along the inferred trajectory. A trajectory graph has no inherent direction: the same graph can be interpreted from either end. Therefore, the root must be selected using biological knowledge or an explicit computational criterion.

By default, the pipeline uses `root_method = "auto"` to automatically select the root. This method identifies the tree tip with the highest mean number of detected genes per cell (`nFeature_RNA`). This approach is based on Gulati et al. (2020), who used transcriptional diversity (the number of detected genes) as an indicator of developmental potential (21). Cells with higher transcriptional diversity may represent less differentiated states and are therefore potential candidates for the starting point of a developmental trajectory. When multiple cell types are included in the analysis, the root selection is restricted to cells belonging to `ROOT_CLUSTER`. This ensures that the starting point is located within the cell type specified by the user.

Users can also customize the root selection criteria using two additional parameters. The `root_score` parameter can specify a cell-level observation column (`obs`) or a gene identifier to guide root selection; set `root_lowest = True` when an end-state marker is expected to have lower expression at the root. The different root selection methods (`auto`, `score`, `most_connected`, `medoid` and `tip`) are described in Supplementary Section S4.

The trajectory configurations to test are defined in `TRAJECTORY_RUNS`. Each run generates a separate output directory, allowing different parameter settings to be compared without overwriting previous results. The example configuration uses 100 nodes, `sigma = 0.1`, `lambda_value = 100`, `eigs = 3`, and `seed = 3`.

The `eigs = 3` parameter specifies that three diffusion components are used to represent cell-state relationships before fitting the trajectory. The remaining parameters control aspects of trajectory construction and fitting; their effects should be evaluated by comparing the resulting graphs and pseudotime patterns.

```python
ROOT_CLUSTER = "Epidermis Cotyledon"

TRAJECTORY_RUNS = [
    trajectory_run(nodes=100, sigma=0.1, lambda_value=100, eigs=3, seed=3),
]

adata_traj, selected_trajectory_dir, trajectory_runs = run_trajectory_runs(
    adata=adata,
    clusters=TRAJECTORY_CLUSTERS,
    root_cluster=ROOT_CLUSTER,
    annotation_col=ANNOTATION_COL,
    output_base_dir=dir_pseudotime,
    runs=TRAJECTORY_RUNS,
)
```

The outputs include the inferred trajectory graph, a pseudotime visualization, and a plot showing the selected root cell **(Figure 16)**. Results are saved under `results/09_pseudotime/`, within the output folder corresponding to each trajectory run.

### Step 4.5. Plotting gene expression along the trajectory {-}

This step visualizes the expression of selected genes along the inferred cotyledon epidermis trajectory. The `plot_genes_on_trajectory()` function takes a list of gene identifiers and, optionally, panel titles. To examine a different marker or compare several genes, simply modify the gene list and provide the corresponding titles if needed.

In this workflow, the analysis focuses on *ATML1*, a marker associated with epidermal cell identity. In the expression matrix, *ATML1* is identified by its *Arabidopsis thaliana* locus code, AT4G21750. Therefore, the function uses AT4G21750 as input while the plot label identifies the gene as *ATML1*.

```python
plot_genes_on_trajectory(
    adata_traj,
    genes=["AT4G21750"],
    titles=["ATML1 (AT4G21750)"],
    run_dir=selected_trajectory_dir,
)
```

The resulting figure shows the distribution of *ATML1* expression across the inferred trajectory, helping visualize how its expression varies among cells positioned along the trajectory **(Figure 17)**. The plot is saved automatically in the corresponding run directory under `gene_plots/`, with a filename based on the plotted gene identifiers. For this example, the output is `gene_plots/trajectory_gene_AT4G21750.pdf`. When multiple genes are plotted, their identifiers are joined with underscores in the filename. The output path is also printed by the function.

**Interpretation note:** The plot describes gene expression in relation to the inferred trajectory and its pseudotime ordering. It does not, by itself, establish that *ATML1* expression changes causally drive cell differentiation or that the inferred trajectory represents a confirmed developmental lineage.

### Step 4.6. Gene expression trends along pseudotime {-}

This step identifies genes whose expression patterns are associated with pseudotime along the inferred cotyledon epidermis trajectory. The function tests genes for association with pseudotime, fits smooth expression curves to capture changes along the trajectory, ranks genes according to their trend signal, and generates heatmaps to visualize the resulting expression patterns.

The analysis uses the trajectory inferred in Step 4.4, with the following parameters: `nodes = 100`, `sigma = 0.1`, `lambda = 100`, `eigs = 3`, and `seed = 3`.

`TOP_N` resulting trend heatmaps help reveal genes with changing expression patterns along pseudotime and identify candidate genes associated with transitions in cell state **(Figure 18)**.

```python
SPLINE_DF = 3

adata_fitted = compute_gene_trends(
    adata_traj,
    selected_trajectory_dir,
    n_jobs=N_JOBS,
    spline_df=SPLINE_DF,
)
```

```python
TOP_N = 10
HIGHLIGHT_GENES = ["AT4G21750"]
ORDERING = "max"

adata_fitted = plot_gene_trends(
    adata_fitted,
    selected_trajectory_dir,
    custom_genes=HIGHLIGHT_GENES,
    top_n=TOP_N,
    ordering=ORDERING,
    adata=adata_traj,
    n_jobs=N_JOBS,
)
```

**Interpretation note:** An association between gene expression and pseudotime indicates that expression varies along the inferred trajectory; it does not establish causality or prove a developmental sequence. The ranking reflects the trend statistic used by the function, so highly ranked genes should be interpreted as candidates for further biological investigation.

This section saves the final AnnData object after trajectory inference and gene-trend analysis. # Notes

1. Expected output: `ls /workspace/fastq/CRA010863` should show the four downloaded `.gz` files plus the four renamed symlinks (`ScWT_S1_L001_R1_001.fastq.gz`, etc.). Cell Ranger reads the symlink names, not the original ones, so if a rename step is skipped or misspelled, the next command below fails immediately with a “no input FASTQs found” error.

2. Expected output: this creates a folder named `Ara/` (matching `--genome`) containing the indexed reference Cell Ranger needs, and ends with a line reading `>>> Reference successfully created! <<<`. This only needs to be built once; the same `Ara/` folder is reused for every sample below.

3. Expected output: each run creates a folder named after `--id` (`ScWT/`, `Scpifq/`) containing `outs/`, and ends with `Pipestance completed successfully!`. Inside `outs/`, `web_summary.html` is a self-contained QC report worth opening first (cell count, reads/cell, sequencing saturation); `filtered_feature_bc_matrix/` is the per-cell count matrix this whole pipeline is built on, and its path is what goes into the sample manifest in Step 1. This is the slowest step here, taking roughly 30-60 minutes per sample.

# Supplementary methods {-}

The steps below are optional. They start from the annotation of Step 2.5
and write their results to separate columns (`celltype_grouped`,
`celltype_curated`) or figures, so the main workflow runs without them. If you
use one of them, set the annotation column of Supplementary Section S1 accordingly. The code is
also available in `workflow/step1_supplementary.R`.

## Supplementary Section S1 - Cell-type grouping {-}

This optional section simplifies annotation labels by merging selected cell types
or subclusters into broader groups. It uses the `grouping` object as a small
renaming table: the names on the left are the current labels, and the values on
the right are the new labels.

For example, in this report the two mesophyll subclusters, `Mesophyll.1` and
`.2`, are renamed as `Mesophyll`. Any cell type that is not listed in `grouping` keeps its
original label.

Use this section when the detailed annotation is useful for inspection but a
simpler grouping is better for figures or downstream summaries. The grouped
labels are stored in `celltype_grouped`, and the grouped UMAP is saved as
`results/05_curation/umap_grouped.pdf`.

```{r supp_s2_cell_type_grouping_optional, strip_comments=FALSE}
# Merge the two mesophyll subclusters into a single label
grouping <- c(
  "Mesophyll.1" = "Mesophyll",
  "Mesophyll.2" = "Mesophyll"
)

output_dir <- dir_05

current <- as.character(ath_sc$celltype)
ath_sc$celltype_grouped <- ifelse(
  current %in% names(grouping), grouping[current], current
)

save_pdf(
  plot_umap(ath_sc, "celltype_grouped"),
  "umap_grouped.pdf"
)

message("\nOK S1 COMPLETE: Cell-type grouping")
```

Representative output from Supplementary Section S1:

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.30\linewidth]{assets/umap_grouped.png}
\end{center}
```

\small
**Figure S1.** UMAP colored by grouped cell-type labels.
\normalsize



## Supplementary Section S2 - Subcluster inspection and manual curation {-}

This optional section is for manual curation when one annotated cluster needs a
closer look. First, `inspect_subcluster_markers()` takes one cluster, splits it
into smaller subclusters, and saves a figure with the subcluster UMAP and marker
gene patterns. This helps decide whether the original label should be kept or
refined.

If refinement is needed, `reassign` is edited as a small mapping table. The outer
name is the cluster being curated, the names inside are subcluster IDs, and the
values are the new labels. The special label `others` is used for any subcluster
not listed explicitly.

In this example the inspected cluster is `Mesophyll.1`, one of the two mesophyll
subclusters that Supplementary Section S1 merges into `Mesophyll`. The inspection
confirms the original label, so `reassign` maps every Mesophyll subcluster back to
`"Mesophyll"` and no cell is relabeled; this is the pattern to use when the
inspection shows that the original annotation was already correct.

The names of `reassign` are looked up in the column given by `annot_col`. Because
`Mesophyll` is a label of `celltype_grouped` (created in Supplementary Section S1)
and not of `celltype`, which only has `Mesophyll.1` and `Mesophyll.2`, the call uses
`annot_col = "celltype_grouped"`; S1 must be run first, otherwise the function stops
with a message that says so.

Then `curate_clusters()` applies those manual labels and stores the result in
`celltype_curated`. The final curated UMAP is saved as
`results/05_curation/umap_curated.pdf`. This block is not executed automatically
because the label choices depend on inspecting the figures.

```{r supp_s3_interactive_cell_type_curation_optional, eval=FALSE, strip_comments=FALSE}
output_dir <- dir_05
Idents(ath_sc) <- "celltype"

# 1. Inspect a cluster (saves the combined subcluster + marker figure)
inspect_subcluster_markers(
  ath_sc, cluster_id = "Mesophyll.1", output_dir = output_dir
)

# 2. Map each cluster's subclusters to labels ("others" = any ID not listed),
#    then curate them in one call. Here Mesophyll's subclusters all map back
#    to "Mesophyll" (no relabeling), which is the pattern to use when the
#    subcluster inspection confirms the original label was already correct.
#    The keys of `reassign` are labels of celltype_grouped (created in
#    Supplementary Section S1), so annot_col and source_col point to that column:
reassign <- list(
  "Mesophyll" = c("others" = "Mesophyll")
)
ath_sc <- curate_clusters(
  ath_sc, reassign, output_dir = output_dir,
  annot_col = "celltype_grouped", source_col = "celltype_grouped"
)

# 3. Save the curated annotation UMAP
save_pdf(
  plot_umap(ath_sc, "celltype_curated"),
  "umap_curated.pdf"
)

message("\nOK S2 COMPLETE: Subcluster inspection and manual curation")
```

Representative output from Supplementary Section S2 — subcluster inspection of the
Mesophyll population (UMAP of its subclusters plus marker-gene panels used to
decide whether to keep or split the label):

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.45\linewidth]{assets/subcluster_markers_mesophyll.png}
\end{center}
```

\small
**Figure S2.** Mesophyll subcluster inspection: subcluster UMAP, marker dotplot, and per-gene marker panels.
\normalsize

*In this example the Mesophyll subclusters are mapped back to `Mesophyll` (no
relabeling), which shows the inspect-then-curate mechanism without changing any
label. The main workflow does not need this step: it continues with the labels
from Step 2.5.*

\newpage

## Supplementary Section S3 - Gene expression violin and feature plots {-}

This optional section shows how to visualize the expression of any gene across the
annotated cell types, in addition to the gene used in Step 2.5. Two plots are drawn: a
violin plot, with the distribution of the expression of the gene in each cell type, and a
FeaturePlot, which colors each cell on the UMAP according to the expression of the gene
and shows directly where in the dataset it is expressed. In Step 2.5, `run_annotation()`
generates both plots for one gene (`gene = "AT4G21750"`, *ATML1*; Figure 10). The same plots
can be made for any other gene, at any time, without repeating the annotation.

To visualize another gene, change the gene identifier (AGI locus code). Several
identifiers can be given as a vector, in which case one panel is drawn per gene. The
figures are saved in `results/04_expression/`.

```r
gene <- "AT4G21750"
gene_tag <- paste(gene, collapse = "_")

output_dir <- dir_04
ath_sc <- JoinLayers(ath_sc)
Idents(ath_sc) <- "celltype"

save_vln(
  plot_gene_violin(ath_sc, gene),
  paste0("vln_gene_", gene_tag, ".pdf")
)
save_pdf(
  plot_gene_umap(ath_sc, gene),
  paste0("feature_gene_", gene_tag, ".pdf")
)

message("\nOK S3 COMPLETE: Gene expression violin and feature plots")
```

Representative output from Supplementary Section S3 (violin plot on the left and
FeaturePlot on the right, as in Figure 10):

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.40\linewidth]{assets/fig10a_violin.png}\hspace{0.03\linewidth}
\includegraphics[width=0.40\linewidth]{assets/fig10b_featureplot.png}
\end{center}
```

## Supplementary Section S4 - Root selection methods {-}

Pseudotime has no direction by itself: the root, where pseudotime is 0, has to be chosen
(Step 4.4). It is set with the `root_method` argument of `run_trajectory_runs()`. Five
methods are available:

| `root_method` | How the root is chosen | When to use it |
|---|---|---|
| `"auto"` (default) | Automatic rule of Gulati et al. (2020) (21), who showed that the number of detected genes per cell is higher in less differentiated cells: the tree tip with the highest mean number of detected genes per cell (`nFeature_RNA`). With several cell types and a `ROOT_CLUSTER`, only the cells of that cell type are scored. | No prior knowledge of the starting point. Cells with more detected genes are assumed to be less differentiated. |
| `"score"` | The same rule as `auto` (Gulati et al. (2020) (21)) with your own `root_score` (a metadata column or a gene); `root_lowest = True` takes the lowest mean instead of the highest. It needs a `ROOT_CLUSTER` that is an existing cell type. | A gene or column marks the start (or the end) of the trajectory better than the number of detected genes. |
| `"most_connected"` | The cell with the highest summed connectivity in the nearest-neighbor graph, among the cells of `ROOT_CLUSTER` (or among all cells if it is empty). It follows the idea that progenitor populations are the most connected in the lineage tree (22), applied here to single cells. | The root must lie inside a cell type chosen by the user. It favors dense regions, which are not always the center. |
| `"medoid"` | The most average cell (the medoid (23)): the cell with the smallest mean distance to all the other cells in PCA space. With a `ROOT_CLUSTER`, only the cells of that cell type are used. | A neutral start in the center of the population. Pseudotime then measures the distance to the center rather than developmental time. |
| `"tip"` | The tree tip with the node number given in `root_tip`. | The biological starting point is known and can be identified in the tree figure (manual override, described below). |

**Manual root override (`"tip"`).**

If the automatic root selection (Step 4.4) does not match the expected
biological starting point, the root can be set manually by specifying a tree
node number. This requires two runs:

1. **First run with `auto`:** Run the trajectory with default settings. The
   pipeline generates an FA (ForceAtlas2) plot showing the tree structure with
   numbered nodes at each tip. Inspect this plot to identify which tip
   corresponds to the biological root (e.g., the progenitor population).

2. **Second run with `tip`:** Re-run with `root_method = "tip"` and `root_tip`
   set to the node number identified in step 1.

```python
# Example: re-run with manual root at node 42
adata_traj, selected_trajectory_dir, trajectory_runs = run_trajectory_runs(
    adata           = adata,
    clusters        = TRAJECTORY_CLUSTERS,
    root_cluster    = ROOT_CLUSTER,
    annotation_col  = ANNOTATION_COL,
    root_method     = "tip",
    root_tip        = 42,  # node number from FA plot
)
```

This approach is useful when the Gulati score (21) (number of detected genes) does
not correctly identify the progenitor population, for example in datasets where
differentiated cells have higher transcriptional diversity than progenitors.
